cues.text: A Brilliant, Combative Master

By the 1130s, Peter Abelard was the most celebrated, and most controversial, theological teacher in France, famous for a dialectical method that subjected even the mysteries of faith to rigorous logical analysis.
He had already been condemned once before, at the Council of Soissons in 1121, for teaching judged to compromise the doctrine of the Trinity.
His continued willingness to apply reason boldly to theological questions drew renewed alarm from more traditionally minded churchmen over the following two decades.
Bernard's Opposition
St. Bernard of Clairvaux , by this point the most influential monastic voice in Western Christendom, grew convinced that Abelard's method itself posed a genuine danger.
This danger extended beyond particular conclusions he reached, subjecting revealed mysteries to a rationalism Bernard believed could only erode the humility faith properly required.

After private admonitions failed to move Abelard, Bernard denounced his teaching to the bishops of France and, at Abelard's own request for a public hearing, agreed to confront him at a council convened at Sens in 1141.
A Council, Not a Debate
Abelard had hoped for genuine theological disputation before the assembled bishops.
On the evening before the council opened, Bernard met privately with them and secured agreement on propositions drawn from Abelard's writings.
These were to be condemned outright rather than debated.

When these propositions were read aloud the following morning, Abelard, sensing the outcome had already been settled beforehand, declined to defend himself at all and instead announced his intention to appeal the matter directly to Rome.
An Appeal That Arrived Too Late
Bernard, undeterred by Abelard's appeal, wrote immediately and forcefully to members of the Roman Curia.
Pope Innocent II confirmed the council's condemnation before Abelard, traveling toward Rome, had gotten further than the abbey of Cluny—a decree that reached him there rather than in Rome itself.

Modern scholarship has noted that several of the nineteen propositions condemned reflected distortions or misreadings of Abelard's actual, more carefully qualified positions rather than his considered teaching in its full context.
Legacy
The Venerable Peter , abbot of Cluny, took up Abelard's case with Rome and secured a mitigation of the sentence.
He reconciled the aging scholar with Bernard himself, offering him a peaceful final home at Cluny, where Abelard spent his remaining months as a monk before his death in 1142.
Sens stands, even in the Church's own retrospective judgment, as a genuinely difficult case.

A real and serious theological concern about the limits of rationalist method met with a process that, in the eyes of most later historians, allowed personal conviction and institutional pressure to substitute.
This replaced the fair, open hearing Abelard had originally sought.
